💧Fluid & Electrolyte Disorders9 items▾

Recall
Chvostek sign and Trousseau sign → which electrolyte disorders?
tap to flip
Answer
May occur with hypomagnesemia / hypocalcemia.
Board trap · Refractory K or Ca — check MgRefractory hypokalemia or hypocalcemia should prompt magnesium correction. Tempting: keep giving more potassium. Do NOT treat refractory K solely with more K when Mg is low.
  • ✎Symptomatic hyponatremia, often at Na ≤ mEq/L → controlled saline.
  • ✎Hyponatremia correction limit: no more than mEq/L in the first 24 h, then mEq/L per 24 h thereafter (European guideline 2014); keep to mEq/L per 24 h or less when the risk of osmotic demyelination is high (US expert panel 2013). Classic textbook: no faster than 1 mEq/L/h or 12 mEq/L/day.
Board trap · Rapid sodium correctionOverrapid correction of hyponatremia → osmotic demyelination (timing is neurologic rather than a fixed postoperative day). Do NOT correct chronic sodium disorders rapidly; chronic hypernatremia is corrected even more slowly.
Recall
Study of choice for a fluid–electrolyte disorder?
tap to flip
Answer
Serum electrolytes + osmolality + renal function.
ECG is critical with potassium abnormalities.
Recall
Severe symptomatic Na/K/Ca/Mg derangement: when to operate, when to wait?
tap to flip
Answer
Operate now only if the surgical disease itself is emergent — correct the life-threatening electrolyte disturbance concurrently.
Elective surgery → observe/optimize first.
  • ★Electrolyte disorders have no primary operation — the treatment is physiologic correction.
Recall
Central venous access: classic structures at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
Carotid artery or pleura (pleural dome), depending on the route/site.

⚗️Acid–Base Balance8 items▾

Recall
Kussmaul respirations indicate?
tap to flip
Answer
Compensatory hyperventilation in metabolic acidosis.
Winter formula (expected respiratory compensation)
Expected PaCO₂ = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8
Predicts the PaCO₂ expected for a given HCO₃⁻ in metabolic acidosis.
HCO₃⁻ 12 → 1.5 × 12 + 8 = 18 + 8 = 26 mmHg expected PaCO₂.
Anion gap
AG = Na − (Cl + HCO₃⁻)
Classic textbook normal: less than about 12 mmol/L.
Na 140, Cl 100, HCO₃⁻ 14 → 140 − (100 + 14) = 26 mmol/L (elevated).
Base deficit as a shock-severity marker
SeverityBase deficitAnswer
Mild−3 to −5
Moderate−6 to −9
Severe≤−10
🧠 Memory toolBase-deficit severity steps
3Mild starts at −3 (−3 to −5)
6Moderate starts at −6 (−6 to −9)
10Severe at −10 or worse
Number hook: 3 – 6 – 10.
Recall
Lactic acidosis from uncontrolled hemorrhage or a surgically correctable septic focus → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Operate now — source control (control the bleeding / septic focus).
Board trap · Bicarbonate for hemorrhagic lactic acidosisTempting: give bicarbonate for lactic acidosis of shock. Right: restore circulation/perfusion (volume) + source control — do NOT substitute bicarbonate for restoring perfusion.
Recall
Top complication of persistent acidosis?
tap to flip
Answer
Myocardial depression, coagulopathy, MODS — no fixed postoperative day.

🔥Endocrine & Metabolic Response to Injury7 items▾

Recall
Stress response to injury: which hormones rise?
tap to flip
Answer
↑ Catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon.
Recall
Metabolic effects of the stress-hormone surge (5)?
tap to flip
Answer
Insulin resistance, lipolysis, gluconeogenesis, proteolysis, negative nitrogen balance.
Recall
What to monitor in the injured/stressed surgical patient?
tap to flip
Answer
Glucose, electrolytes, phosphate, Mg, weight/intake trends, organ function.
No operative scoring system applies here.
Board trap · Stress hyperglycemia before emergency surgeryTempting: postpone the operation until glucose is normal. Right: life-saving surgery should not be delayed merely to normalize stress hyperglycemia.
Recall
Elective surgery + major uncontrolled endocrine disease → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Observe/optimize first, when correction is feasible.
Recall
Top complication of the catabolic response?
tap to flip
Answer
Catabolism → muscle loss, infection risk, delayed wound healing; no fixed postoperative day.
Board trap · Overfeeding to reverse the stress responseAVOID aggressive overfeeding as a strategy to “reverse” the stress response.

🩸Shock & Hemorrhage Classes12 items▾

  • ★Board rule: when physiology and imaging conflict in an unstable surgical patient, physiology usually determines whether to operate now — prioritize the immediate operative or resuscitative decision.
Hemorrhagic shock classification (ATLS 10th ed, 2018)
ClassBlood lossHRBPPulse pressureCNSBase deficitDecisionAnswer
I<750 mL / <15%Normal
Classic: <100		NormalNormalNormal GCS0 to −2 mEq/LObserve response; crystalloid/blood as clinically needed
II750–1500 mL / 15–30%Normal or ↑
Classic: 100–120		NormalNarrowedNormal GCS
Classic: anxious		−2 to −6 mEq/LEscalate resuscitation; blood products possible
III1500–2000 mL / 30–40%↑
Classic: 120–140		Normal or ↓
Classic: hypotension		NarrowedGCS ↓
Classic: confused		−6 to −10 mEq/LBlood products + rapid source control
IV>2000 mL / >40%↑↑
Classic: >140		↓ (severe hypotension)NarrowedGCS ↓
Classic: obtunded/lethargic		−10 mEq/L or worseMassive transfusion + immediate hemorrhage control
🧠 Memory toolHemorrhage class cut-offs (% blood loss)
15Class I: below 15% (<750 mL)
30Class II: 15–30% (750–1500 mL)
40Class III: 30–40% (1500–2000 mL)
GameClass IV: above 40% (>2000 mL)
Tennis score: 15 – 30 – 40 – game. Classic HR steps: <100, 100–120, 120–140, >140. ATLS 10 replaced the fixed HR/BP numbers with trends and added base-deficit bands (2 – 6 – 10). Most tested: in class II the systolic BP is still normal — only the pulse pressure narrows; hypotension begins in class III.
🩺 Think it through
Trauma patient is confused and hypotensive with HR above 120. Which hemorrhage class, and what is needed?
Class III (1500–2000 mL / 30–40%) → blood products + rapid source control. Falling BP and a depressed GCS/confusion mark class III (base deficit −6 to −10 mEq/L); obtundation with HR >140 would be class IV.
Board trap · Normal heart rate does not exclude bleedingTachycardia is not sufficiently sensitive to exclude hemorrhage — a normal HR does not reassure.
Recall
Imaging of choice in trauma: unstable abdomen vs stable/stabilized high-energy trauma?
tap to flip
Answer
Unstable abdomen → FAST.
Stable/stabilized high-energy trauma → contrast CT.
Board trap · CT first in the unstable bleeding patientTempting: send unstable hemorrhagic trauma to CT first. Contraindicated — CT transport for a persistently unstable bleeding patient must not delay source control in persistent shock. Right: hemorrhage localization/control first.
Recall
Nonresponder or transient responder with suspected surgically controllable hemorrhage → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Operate now — persistent nonresponse → source control.
Recall
Hemodynamically stable responder in hemorrhagic shock → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Define the injury; observe/nonoperative management if the injury is amenable to close observation ± embolization.
  • ★Procedure of choice in hemorrhagic shock depends on the bleeding site: laparotomy / thoracotomy / vascular intervention. In exsanguinating abdominal trauma, hemorrhage control precedes reconstruction.
Recall
Top complication after prolonged shock?
tap to flip
Answer
MODS — no single fixed postoperative day.
Board trap · Crystalloids indefinitelyTempting: keep running crystalloid in massive hemorrhage. Right: blood-product resuscitation + hemorrhage control.

🚑Trauma: ATLS, GCS & Damage Control11 items▾

🧠 Memory toolATLS primary survey — xABCDE (ATLS 11th ed, 2025)
xeXsanguinating external hemorrhage — control it first (direct pressure, tourniquet, wound packing, pelvic binder)
AAirway + C-spine protection
BBreathing and ventilation
CCirculation + hemorrhage control
DDisability / GCS
EExposure + prevent hypothermia
Classic textbook and older board questions: plain ABCDE. The only change in order is that life-threatening external bleeding is stopped before the airway step.
Glasgow Coma Scale (used in early trauma assessment)
ComponentMaximumAnswer
Eyes4
Verbal5
Motor6
Total3–15
🧠 Memory toolGCS maximum points
4Eyes
5Verbal
6Motor
4 – 5 – 6 in the order E, V, M; total runs 3–15.
  • ✎GCS ≤ is a classic threshold for considering definitive airway protection.
Trauma: operate now vs observe
ScenarioOperate / intervene nowObserve / continue workupAnswer
Any trauma patientShock + peritonitis; uncontrolled hemorrhage; unstable abdominal patient with positive FASTStable solid-organ injury meeting nonoperative criteria — with monitoring and immediate access to intervention
Blunt abdominal traumaUnstable: positive FAST + shock → laparotomyStable → CT ± nonoperative management
Penetrating traumaShock, peritonitis, uncontrolled bleedingSelected stable patient → directed evaluation
🩺 Think it through
Blunt abdominal trauma; the patient is in shock and FAST is positive. CT or operating room?
Laparotomy now — an unstable abdomen with a positive FAST is operated on; CT ± nonoperative management is for the stable patient.
Recall
Failure of nonoperative management — 4 signs?
tap to flip
Answer
New hypotension, rising transfusion requirement, peritonitis, worsening lactate/base deficit.
Damage control vs definitive repair
ParameterDamage control nowDefinitive repair now/laterAnswer
TemperatureHypothermia <35°CNormothermic
Acid–baseArterial pH <7.2Corrected acidosis
Base deficitSevere/marked base deficit, e.g. >15 mmol/L (classic textbook damage-control discussion)Restored perfusion
CoagulationSevere/refractory coagulopathyCorrected coagulation
HemodynamicsExsanguinating physiologyHemodynamic reserve adequate for reconstruction
GoalStop bleeding + contaminationFinal anatomic reconstruction
What is doneAbbreviated surgery: packing, contamination control, temporary closureDefinitive repair after physiologic normalization in the ICU (temperature, perfusion, coagulation and acid–base status restored)
🧠 Memory toolDamage-control triggers (lethal triad)
HHypothermia — below 35°C
AAcidosis — pH below 7.2, severe base deficit
CCoagulopathy — severe/refractory
All three present → abbreviate the operation.
Board trap · Long reconstruction in a crashing patientContraindicated: prolonged definitive reconstruction in a patient spiraling into hypothermia–acidosis–coagulopathy.
Recall
Pringle maneuver: what is encircled, and what is at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
Encircles the portal triad — portal vein, hepatic artery and common bile duct lie within the pedicle.
Careless application risks the common bile duct/portal structures.

🔥Burns: TBSA, Fluids & Escharotomy10 items▾

Rule of Nines — estimates adult TBSA
Adult region%TBSAAnswer
Head/neck9%
Each arm9%
Anterior trunk18%
Posterior trunk18%
Each leg18%
Perineum1%
🧠 Memory toolRule of Nines adds up to 100
9Head/neck
9 × 2Arms (9 each)
18 × 2Anterior + posterior trunk
18 × 2Legs (18 each)
1Perineum
9 + 18 + 36 + 36 + 1 = 100%.
Recall
Full-thickness vs partial-thickness burn — appearance?
tap to flip
Answer
Full thickness: leathery, nonblanching, relatively painless.
Partial thickness: blistering, wet, painful.
Burn resuscitation starting formula (ABA 2023)
Fluid in first 24 h = 2 mL × kg × %TBSA of lactated Ringer — a starting estimate, then titrate hourly to urine output
Half in the first 8 h counted from the time of burn; the remainder over the next 16 h.
Classic textbook (Parkland / Baxter): 3–4 mL × kg × %TBSA, same 8 h / 16 h split.
70 kg, 40% TBSA: 2 × 70 × 40 = 5,600 mL → 2,800 mL in the first 8 h (350 mL/h), 2,800 mL over the next 16 h (175 mL/h). Parkland at 4 mL would give 4 × 70 × 40 = 11,200 mL (5,600 + 5,600).
  • ✎The ABA (2023) starting rate is mL/kg/%TBSA rather than Parkland's , because the older estimates led to excessive fluid administration.
  • ✎Burn resuscitation endpoint: titrate fluid to an adult urine output of mL/kg/h, about mL/h (ABA; ATLS). Classic textbook: urine output ≈30 mL/h and MAP ≈60 mmHg.
Board trap · Formula-driven fluid without reassessmentContraindicated: formula-driven fluid without endpoint reassessment. Overresuscitation → compartment syndromes / pleural effusions, usually during early resuscitation.
Board trap · Escharotomy vs fasciotomyCircumferential burn/eschar with vascular (or ventilatory) compromise → escharotomy now; more fluid alone is wrong when restriction is the problem. Adequate perfusion/ventilation → close reassessment.
True deep compartment syndrome: escharotomy only is wrong → fasciotomy.
Recall
Burn depth → observe or operate?
tap to flip
Answer
Observe / wound care: superficial and many superficial partial-thickness burns.
Excision + skin grafting (when indicated): deep partial-thickness/full-thickness wounds unlikely to heal.
Board trap · Waiting on the burn airwayHoarseness, stridor, dyspnea, progressive airway edema → early endotracheal intubation. Tempting and contraindicated: waiting for obvious/complete obstruction before intubating a progressively edematous burn airway.

🩹Wound Healing & Dehiscence9 items▾

  • ★Phases of wound healing: hemostasis/inflammation → proliferation → maturation/remodeling.
Recall
Named categories of wound closure?
tap to flip
Answer
Primary, secondary, and tertiary (delayed primary) intention.
  • ✎A healed wound regains at most about % of the strength of uninjured tissue — never 100% — reached at about months. Classic textbook: maximal around 6 weeks, ultimately 75–80%.
Recall
Classic structure at risk in wound failure?
tap to flip
Answer
Fascia — failure produces evisceration / incisional hernia.
  • ✎Top wound complication: ; classic board timing POD .
Board trap · Evisceration managed at the bedsideFascial dehiscence/evisceration: bedside reduction and dressing only is wrong. Right: protect viscera → resuscitate → urgent OR for operative reclosure.
Recall
Superficial skin separation, fascia intact, no deep infection → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Observe.
Recall
Operative principles for a contaminated or necrotic wound?
tap to flip
Answer
Debridement of necrotic tissue; delayed closure when contamination requires initial open management.
Board trap · Closing over infectionContraindicated: primary closure over uncontrolled infection or devitalized tissue.

🦠Surgical Infection & Wound Classes9 items▾

Surgical wound classification (Class I–IV contamination)
ClassDefinition / exampleDecision relevanceAnswer
I CleanNo infected field / no hollow viscus enteredLowest SSI risk
II Clean-contaminatedControlled entry into respiratory/GI/GU tractProphylaxis indicated
III ContaminatedMajor contamination / traumatic wound / spillageHigher SSI risk; treatment strategy escalates
IV DirtyEstablished infection / perforated viscus / necrotizing infectionTreat as established infection, not prophylaxis
🧠 Memory toolWound classes in order
IClean
IIClean-contaminated
IIIContaminated
IVDirty
Each step adds contamination: nothing entered → controlled entry → spillage → established infection.
Recall
Clinical clues to a surgical infection (no single sensitive named maneuver)?
tap to flip
Answer
Purulence, fluctuance, crepitus, disproportionate pain.
Recall
Imaging of choice for an occult deep/organ-space collection?
tap to flip
Answer
CT — in a stable patient.
Recall
Surgical infection: operate now for which 3?
tap to flip
Answer
Necrotizing soft-tissue infection, uncontrolled perforation, drainable abscess requiring surgical drainage.
Board trap · Imaging before debridement in necrotizing infectionNecrotizing infection → immediate aggressive debridement (operative source control) when clinically established; never routine observation. Tempting and wrong: waiting for CT/extensive imaging in an unstable patient with obvious necrotizing infection.
Board trap · Antibiotics alone for an abscessAbscess → incision and drainage. Treating an abscess with antibiotics alone is contraindicated — it needs drainage/source control.
Recall
Which infections can be observed / managed medically?
tap to flip
Answer
Cellulitis without collection; selected contained infection suitable for antibiotics ± image-guided drainage.
  • ✎SSI commonly becomes evident around POD — several days after operation rather than immediately (classic textbook: POD 7–10). CDC surveillance window: within days, or days when an implant is placed.

🧼Asepsis, Antisepsis & Prophylaxis5 items▾

Recall
Prophylactic antibiotic: when must the drug be on board?
tap to flip
Answer
Adequate drug concentration must be present at incision; late administration after contamination is less effective.
Recall
When to redose the prophylactic antibiotic?
tap to flip
Answer
Lengthy cases exceeding the antibiotic half-life, or major blood loss/fluid replacement.
Recall
Asepsis: is there an operation? What is observed?
tap to flip
Answer
No primary operation unless contamination has produced a drainable/invasive infection.
Uncomplicated clean wound with standard prophylaxis → observe.
Recall
Why are mesh, valves and prostheses the classic structures at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
Contamination of an implant may establish biofilm.
Board trap · Prolonged “prophylaxis”Contraindicated: prolonged “prophylaxis” as a substitute for drainage/source control.

🍽️Surgical Nutrition9 items▾

  • ✎Practical initial caloric estimate for many critically ill adults: kcal/kg/day.
🧠 Memory toolRoute of feeding
Gut functionalEnteral nutrition — route of choice
Gut inaccessible / nonfunctional, or needs not met enterallyTPN
If the gut works, use it.
Recall
TPN is reserved for?
tap to flip
Answer
Inaccessible/nonfunctional GI tract, or inability to meet requirements enterally.
Recall
Refeeding syndrome → hallmark and danger?
tap to flip
Answer
Severe hypophosphatemia, potentially respiratory failure.
Board trap · Full calories on day oneContraindicated: aggressive full-calorie feeding immediately in a severely malnourished patient at refeeding risk.
  • ★Nutrition needs no routine imaging; feeding-tube position requires appropriate confirmation according to the route.
Recall
When to place a feeding gastrostomy/jejunostomy?
tap to flip
Answer
When prolonged enteral access is required and anatomy/clinical context justify it.
Recall
Jejunostomy: classic structure at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
Mesenteric blood supply.
Recall
Top complication of TPN?
tap to flip
Answer
Catheter sepsis or electrolyte disturbance; no fixed postoperative day.

🅾️Blood Transfusion & Hemostasis8 items▾

Recall
Focal operative bleeding vs diffuse oozing?
tap to flip
Answer
Focal → suspect a mechanical cause.
Diffuse oozing → consider coagulopathy.
  • ✎Massive-trauma resuscitation is balanced: plasma : platelets : RBC.
  • ✎In an actively bleeding patient keep platelets above about × 10⁹/L.
Recall
Studies of choice in a bleeding/coagulopathic patient?
tap to flip
Answer
CBC, PT/INR, aPTT, fibrinogen ± TEG/ROTEM.
Recall
Ongoing surgically controllable hemorrhage despite resuscitation → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Operate now: direct hemorrhage control + massive transfusion protocol, not transfusion alone.
The structure at risk is the bleeding vessel itself — source control outranks laboratory normalization.
Transfusion complications by timing
ComplicationTiming / featuresAnswer
Acute transfusion reaction (top complication)During / immediately after transfusion
Massive transfusionEarly hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy
Post-transfusion purpura (delayed)Around day 5–6
  • ✎Post-transfusion purpura appears around day .
Board trap · Continuing blood during a suspected reactionTempting: continue the blood while observing. Contraindicated when an acute hemolytic/transfusion reaction is suspected → stop the transfusion immediately.

🎗️Surgical Oncology Principles8 items▾

🧠 Memory toolTNM staging
TTumor
NNodes
MMetastasis
Exact cut-offs are organ-specific, not universal.
Recall
Staging imaging before cancer surgery?
tap to flip
Answer
Tumor-specific staging CT/MRI/PET as appropriate; obtain distant staging before major surgery when metastatic risk could alter intent.
Recall
When is cancer surgery indicated (absolute operative principle)?
tap to flip
Answer
Resectable malignancy for which surgery offers cure/control (curative or palliative indication) and an R0 / negative-margin resection is achievable.
Recall
Procedure of choice for a resectable tumor?
tap to flip
Answer
En bloc tumor resection with appropriate margin ± regional lymph-node management.
Recall
Unresectable/metastatic cancer → operate?
tap to flip
Answer
Observe/systemic treatment first — unless surgery is needed for bleeding, obstruction, infection, perforation, or palliation.
  • ★In cancer surgery the structures at risk are organ-specific (regional nerves/vessels and the lymphatic basin), and the top complication is site-specific with no universal postoperative day.
Board trap · Smaller operation at the cost of marginsContraindicated: tumor violation/fragmentation, or sacrificing oncologic margins merely to perform a smaller procedure.
Board trap · Bigger is not betterTempting: the largest possible operation regardless of margins/morbidity. More radical surgery is not automatically better if adequate negative margins can be obtained with a less morbid operation → oncologically adequate negative-margin resection.

🛡️Surgical Immunology7 items▾

Recall
Postoperative inflammation vs infection — key distinction?
tap to flip
Answer
Inflammation ≠ infection; immunosuppressed patients may show muted signs.
Recall
Imaging for suspected infection in the immunocompromised surgical patient?
tap to flip
Answer
Imaging directed at the suspected site of infection. No surgical score determines operation.
Recall
Immunosuppressed patient: operate now for?
tap to flip
Answer
Abscess, necrosis, perforation, graft-threatening technical complication — immunosuppression does not remove the need for source control.
Recall
Immune dysregulation without a surgical cause → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Observe / medical management.
Recall
Too much vs too little immunosuppression?
tap to flip
Answer
Excessive → infection / malignancy.
Inadequate → rejection.
  • ★Top complication in the immunosuppressed patient is infection; timing varies.
Board trap · Reflex increase in immunosuppressionContraindicated: reflexively increasing immunosuppression for graft dysfunction before excluding infection/technical causes.

🫘Transplantation & Rejection7 items▾

Types of graft rejection
Rejection typeTiming conceptKey featureImmediate decisionAnswer
HyperacuteImmediate / very earlyPreformed antibody–mediated graft failureUrgent graft assessment; often irreversible
AcuteEarly to laterCellular and/or antibody mediatedConfirm, often with biopsy; intensify directed immunotherapy
ChronicMonths–yearsProgressive vascular/fibrotic lossLong-term graft-management strategy
Recall
Acute graft dysfunction with concern for thrombosis or inflow/outflow failure — imaging?
tap to flip
Answer
Graft-specific Doppler / vascular imaging.
Recall
Transplant: operate now for?
tap to flip
Answer
Vascular thrombosis, uncontrolled bleeding, leak, torsion/technical catastrophe threatening graft viability → urgent graft salvage/revision for a technical vascular complication.
Recall
Stable graft dysfunction, technical complications excluded → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Observe / treat medically — reversible medication or immunologic issue.
Recall
Kidney transplant: classic structures at risk?
tap to flip

DecisionWhen / whatAnswer
1° / superficial viable injuryOBSERVE
Stop observing whenPerforation, necrosis, sepsis
Questionable deep injuryExplore / second look

Recall

tap to flip
Answer
Salmon-colored distal columnar mucosa.
Test of choice: EGD with systematic biopsy — diagnosis requires biopsy demonstrating intestinal metaplasia.
Barrett: histology → decision (ACG 2022)
FindingDecisionAnswer
No dysplasiaSurveillance endoscopy (observe / endoscopic pathway): every 5 years if segment <3 cm, every 3 years if ≥3 cm
Indefinite for dysplasiaIncrease PPI to twice daily, then repeat endoscopy with biopsy within 6 months
Low-grade dysplasia (confirmed)Endoscopic eradication therapy to reduce progression; acceptable alternative = surveillance EGD at 6 months, 12 months, then yearly. Classic textbook: high-dose acid suppression, then repeat biopsy
High-grade dysplasia / intramucosal disease (appropriately selected superficial neoplasia)Endoscopic eradication: EMR ± radiofrequency ablation
Invasive T1b or deeper cancerConsider esophagectomy (definitive resection)
Selected multifocal/long-segment disease unsuitable for endoscopic controlEsophagectomy

🔥Acute Cholangitis10 items▾

🧠 Memory toolCharcot triad → Reynolds pentad
1Fever
2RUQ / epigastric pain
3Jaundice
+4Shock
+5Altered mental status
1–3 = Charcot triad, present in only about two-thirds — its absence does not exclude cholangitis. All 5 = Reynolds pentad → severe septic cholangitis.
Recall
Cholangitis: what determines urgency?
tap to flip
Answer
Hemodynamic instability, organ failure, altered mentation and persistent sepsis — graded formally by the Tokyo Guidelines 2018 severity grades.
Acute cholangitis severity (Tokyo Guidelines 2018)
GradeCriteriaBiliary drainageAnswer
III — severeDysfunction of ≥1 organ system: cardiovascular (hypotension needing dopamine ≥5 µg/kg/min or any norepinephrine), neurological (disturbed consciousness), respiratory (PaO₂/FiO₂ <300), renal (oliguria or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL), hepatic (PT-INR >1.5), hematological (platelets <100,000/mm³)Urgent drainage with organ support
II — moderateNo organ dysfunction but any 2 of 5: WBC >12,000 or <4,000/mm³; fever ≥39°C; age ≥75 y; total bilirubin ≥5 mg/dL; albumin <0.7 × lower limit of normalEarly drainage
I — mildMeets neither Grade III nor Grade II criteriaAntibiotics first; drain if no response within 24 h
Recall
Cholangitis: imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
Ultrasound first for stones / ductal dilatation; CT/MRI for a mass or alternate cause.
Imaging should not delay drainage in a septic patient.
Recall
Cholangitis: which findings mean INTERVENE NOW?
tap to flip
Answer
Sepsis with biliary obstruction, Reynolds pentad, worsening organ dysfunction, or persistent obstruction despite antibiotics / resuscitation → urgent ERCP drainage.
  • ★Cholangitis pathway: fever + RUQ pain + jaundice → antibiotics + sepsis resuscitation → ERCP with sphincterotomy ± stone extraction / stent / drainage → if ERCP fails: PTC, EUS-guided drainage, or surgical drainage according to anatomy / expertise → gallstone-related: cholecystectomy after resolution.
  • ✎Cholecystectomy after gallstone cholangitis resolves and the duct is cleared: laparoscopic cholecystectomy within weeks of ERCP (ESGE 2019). Classic textbook: interval cholecystectomy at approximately weeks.
Recall
ERCP: classic structure at risk and top complication (with timing)?
tap to flip
Answer
Pancreatic duct / ampulla → post-ERCP pancreatitis, usually within 6–24 h.
Board trap · Antibiotics without decompressionDo not rely on antibiotics alone when obstruction persists. Antibiotics alone are acceptable only while arranging source control.
Board trap · Cholecystostomy for cholangitisTempting: drain the gallbladder. Wrong — the infection is in the obstructed biliary tree, not the gallbladder. Do not substitute cholecystostomy for common-duct drainage as primary treatment.

🟢Gallstones & Acute Cholecystitis10 items▾

Recall
Murphy sign / sonographic Murphy sign: value and limitation?
tap to flip
Answer
Supports acute cholecystitis; absence does not exclude it, especially in older or diabetic patients.
Recall
Acute cholecystitis: imaging of choice and its findings?
tap to flip
Answer
Ultrasound first: stones, wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy.
If equivocal → HIDA.
  • ✎HIDA: gallbladder nonvisualization after h → obstructed cystic duct, strongly supports acute cholecystitis; normal gallbladder filling argues against it.
Recall
RUQ pain + Murphy sign + gallstones in a fit patient → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Acute cholecystitis → early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
Gangrene, perforation or uncontrolled sepsis makes source control urgent.
  • ✎Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy: as soon as possible, within days of admission and within days of symptom onset (WSES 2020). Classic textbook: preferably within ~ h from onset.
Recall
Acute cholecystitis in a critically ill / unfit patient → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Temporize: IV antibiotics + percutaneous cholecystostomy (about 90% improve) → interval cholecystectomy if indicated.
Recall
Signs that temporizing treatment of cholecystitis has failed?
tap to flip
Answer
Persistent sepsis, gangrene, perforation, clinical deterioration.
🧠 Memory toolCritical view of safety — 3 requirements
1Hepatocystic triangle cleared
2Cystic plate exposed
3Exactly TWO structures seen entering the gallbladder
Preventive maneuver against bile-duct injury.
Recall
Cholecystectomy: classic structure at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Common bile duct / common hepatic duct.
Top complication: bile leak, typically POD 1–7.
Board trap · Blind clipping / blind dissectionWhen anatomy is unclear or the critical view cannot be obtained, do not clip blindly or continue blind hepatocystic dissection — use a bailout / conversion rather than guessing.

🪨Choledocholithiasis8 items▾

Recall
Clinical clue to a common bile duct stone?
tap to flip
Answer
Intermittent biliary pain + jaundice; transient obstruction may behave like a “ball-valve” stone.
  • ✎CBD > mm on ultrasound in a patient with gallstones, jaundice and biliary pain is highly suggestive of CBD stones.
Recall
Uncertain duct stone after ultrasound → next test?
tap to flip
Answer
MRCP or EUS (ultrasound is first).
  • ✎MRCP for CBD stones: sensitivity ~%, specificity ~%.
Recall
Choledocholithiasis: INTERVENE NOW vs observe?
tap to flip
Answer
Now (ERCP): cholangitis, persistent obstruction, or gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis.
Observe: only a selected asymptomatic or uncertain stone while it is evaluated — no prolonged observation if persistent jaundice, cholangitis or pancreatitis develops.
Recall
Choledocholithiasis: procedure of choice (two accepted routes)?
tap to flip
Answer
ERCP with stone extraction followed by cholecystectomy, OR one-stage laparoscopic cholecystectomy + IOC / CBD exploration.
Principle: duct clearance + cholecystectomy.
Recall
CBD stone intervention: classic structures at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
CBD / duodenum / pancreatic ampulla, depending on the intervention.
Board trap · Purely diagnostic ERCPDo not use ERCP purely diagnostically when MRCP / EUS can answer the question and no therapeutic intervention is planned.

🟡Obstructive Jaundice & Perihilar Cholangiocarcinoma10 items▾

Recall
Courvoisier sign?
tap to flip
Answer
Palpable nontender gallbladder + jaundice → suggests pancreatic-head / distal malignant obstruction. Insensitive — its absence means little.
Recall
Cholestatic laboratory pattern?
tap to flip
Answer
Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia + alkaline phosphatase elevation.
  • ★Imaging pathway: ultrasound first → duct dilation + stones → ERCP pathway; duct dilation without stones → contrast CT for malignant obstruction.
Recall
Obstructive jaundice + cholangitis / sepsis → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Urgent biliary drainage (endoscopic / percutaneous) before full oncologic staging; curative resection only after stabilization and staging.
Stable malignant obstruction can be staged first.
Recall
Definitive operation for resectable malignant biliary obstruction?
tap to flip
Answer
Distal → Whipple.
Selected hilar cholangiocarcinoma → bile-duct resection ± hepatectomy according to extent.
Recall
Unresectable / metastatic malignant biliary obstruction → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Palliate: endoscopic metal stent or percutaneous drainage — not radical operation.
Recall
Hilar surgery: structures at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Portal vein / hepatic artery / biliary radicals.
Bile leak after reconstruction, usually POD 3–7.
Board trap · Wrong moves in obstructive jaundice(1) Prolonged / complete cancer staging before drainage in a septic obstructed patient. (2) Major curative resection in metastatic / unresectable disease.
Bismuth-Corlette — perihilar cholangiocarcinoma
TypeExtentOperative decisionAnswer
IBelow hilar confluenceBile-duct resection + reconstruction
IIReaches bifurcationHilar bile-duct resection + reconstruction
IIIaExtends into right hepatic ductRight hepatectomy + bile-duct resection, often caudate
IIIbExtends into left hepatic ductLeft hepatectomy + bile-duct resection, often caudate
IVBilateral proximal involvementFrequently unresectable; transplant protocols only in highly selected patients
🧠 Memory toolBismuth-Corlette type III side
aright hepatic duct → right hepatectomy
bleft hepatic duct → left hepatectomy
The operation follows the extent of ductal involvement.

🍺Cirrhosis — Operative Risk (Child-Pugh & MELD)9 items▾

Recall
Asterixis, caput medusae, Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur → each signifies?
tap to flip
Answer
Asterixis → encephalopathy.
Caput medusae and Cruveilhier-Baumgarten murmur → portal-systemic collateralization.

AAlbumin
BBilirubin

Child-Turcotte-Pugh scoring
Variable1 point2 points3 pointsAnswer
Bilirubin<2 mg/dL2–3>3
Albumin>3.5 g/dL2.8–3.5<2.8
INR<1.71.7–2.2>2.2

Child class → operative decision
ClassScoreOperative reserveAnswer
A5–6Best operative reserve
B7–9Major caution

  • ✎Historical surgical mortality in cirrhosis: roughly % Child A, % Child B, % Child C.
  • ✎MELD and elective surgery: < generally acceptable (like Child A — if otherwise suitable); caution; > avoid elective nontransplant surgery when possible (like Child C).
Recall
Cirrhosis: imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
Doppler ultrasound when portal-vein patency / flow matters; CT/MRI for lesions / anatomy.
Recall
Cirrhotic patient: when to OPERATE vs optimize first?
tap to flip
Answer
Operate: necessary surgery in a compensated, optimized patient when benefit outweighs risk.
Optimize / transplant evaluation first: decompensated ascites, encephalopathy, severe malnutrition, infection, renal dysfunction.
Board trap · Elective nontransplant surgery in decompensationContraindicated: nontransplant surgery in acute fulminant hepatitis or severe decompensated chronic hepatitis. Do not routinely perform elective nontransplant surgery in severe decompensation or MELD >15 without a compelling indication.

🩸Portal Hypertension & Variceal Bleeding8 items▾

Recall
Clinical presentation of variceal bleeding?
tap to flip
Answer
Hematemesis / melena in a cirrhotic; asterixis may reflect associated encephalopathy.
  • ★Variceal bleed sequence: initial stabilization → octreotide + antibiotics → urgent endoscopy with band ligation (first-line) → refractory / recurrent uncontrolled bleeding → TIPS → once controlled: secondary prevention / transplant evaluation.
🩺 Think it through
Cirrhotic with active variceal hemorrhage remains unstable; bleeding is not controlled after octreotide, antibiotics and banding. What now?
Intervene now. Sengstaken-Blakemore balloon tamponade only as a temporary bridge (≤36 h) → definitive rescue with TIPS / transplant pathway.
  • ✎TIPS is dilated until the portal pressure gradient is ≤ mmHg.
Board trap · Balloon tamponade as definitive therapySengstaken-Blakemore tamponade is tempting once bleeding stops. It is for refractory hemorrhage only as a temporary bridge — never definitive, and must not be prolonged >36 hours.
Recall
Ultimate definitive treatment of decompensated portal hypertensive cirrhosis?
tap to flip
Answer
Liver transplantation in suitable patients.
Recall
When are surgical shunts considered for portal hypertension?
tap to flip
Answer
Only in selected MELD <15 patients when TIPS / transplant are unsuitable. Hepatic reserve is judged by CTP / MELD.
Recall
TIPS: structures at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Portal / hepatic vascular structures and bile ducts.
Top complication: hepatic encephalopathy, days–weeks; incidence ~25–30%.

🎗️Hepatocellular Carcinoma7 items▾

Recall
Imaging hallmark of HCC?
tap to flip
Answer
Arterial-phase hyperenhancement + delayed washout; an enhancing portal-vein thrombus strongly suggests HCC.
Recall
HCC: imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
Multiphase CT or contrast MRI.
  • ✎Milan criteria: 1 lesion ≤ cm OR ≤ lesions each ≤ cm, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic spread.
Recall
HCC → resect or transplant?
tap to flip
Answer
Resect: noncirrhotic localized HCC; Child A with preserved function and no portal hypertension → consider resection (resectable disease + adequate reserve).
Transplant: poor hepatic reserve (inadequate for resection) + tumor within Milan criteria.
Recall
HCC not resectable and not a transplant candidate → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Locoregional / systemic pathway.
  • ✎Future liver remnant needed: ~% in normal liver; ~% when the liver is diseased or chemotherapy-exposed.
Board trap · Major hepatectomy with inadequate remnantDo not undertake major resection with an inadequate future liver remnant or severe hepatic decompensation.

🎯Colorectal Liver Metastases & Liver Resection Risks6 items▾

Recall
What primarily determines resectability of colorectal liver metastases?
tap to flip
Answer
What liver remains — not the absolute number of metastases.
Board trap · “Four or more metastases = unresectable”Outdated distractor. Number alone does not exclude resection.
Recall
Colorectal liver metastases: imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
Multiphase CT/MRI ± PET depending on staging needs.
Recall
When to operate on colorectal liver metastases?
tap to flip
Answer
When all gross disease can be removed / ablated while preserving adequate inflow, outflow, biliary drainage and FLR.
Recall
Inadequate FLR before hepatectomy → strategy?
tap to flip
Answer
Portal vein embolization ± staged hepatectomy.
Liver surgery — structure at risk and top complication
SettingStructure at riskTop complication (typical timing)Answer
Hepatectomy in cirrhosisHepatic veins / IVC and portal pediclesPostoperative hepatic decompensation / liver failure — first postoperative week
Major hepatectomy for HCCHepatic veins / IVCPosthepatectomy liver failure — first 3–7 days
Resection of colorectal metastasesHepatic veins / portal pediclesLiver failure or bile leak — POD 3–7

Recall
Acute pancreatitis: role of ultrasound vs CT?
tap to flip
Answer
Ultrasound for a gallstone cause.
CT reserved for deterioration / suspected local complication — not routine early scanning.
Recall
Only indication for urgent ERCP in gallstone pancreatitis?
tap to flip
Answer
Cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction.
Recall
Uncomplicated pancreatitis or sterile necrosis → management?
tap to flip
Answer
Supportive, no operation: fluids, analgesia, early enteral nutrition, organ support.
  • ★Step-up approach: infected necrosis / deterioration → percutaneous / endoscopic drainage first → if drainage fails: delayed minimally invasive necrosectomy → laparotomy only for failed step-up, perforation / bowel ischemia (bowel catastrophe), or rare severe abdominal compartment syndrome.
  • ✎Necrosectomy should ideally be postponed weeks when feasible.
Recall
Necrosectomy: structures at risk; top complications of pancreatitis and of necrosectomy?
tap to flip
Answer
At risk: splenic / portal-mesenteric vessels.
Pancreatitis: infected necrosis, generally after the first week. After necrosectomy: hemorrhage / fistula.
Board trap · Prophylactic antibioticsDo not give routine prophylactic antibiotics for sterile pancreatitis.
Board trap · Early open necrosectomyNecrosis on CT is not by itself an indication — do not perform early open necrosectomy solely because necrosis is present.

🧱Chronic Pancreatitis5 items▾

Chronic pancreatitis — anatomy picks the operation
AnatomyProcedureAnswer
Dilated duct + stones / stenoses (large-duct, decompressive disease)Puestow / Partington-Rochelle longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy
Dominant inflammatory pancreatic-head disease, cancer excludedFrey or Beger

Recall
Chronic pancreatitis: indications for surgery vs nonoperative care?
tap to flip
Answer
Operate: intractable pain despite medical / endoscopic therapy, obstructed dilated duct, inflammatory head mass, biliary / duodenal obstruction, symptomatic complication, or malignancy concern.
Observe: controlled symptoms → medical / endoscopic treatment.
Recall
Chronic pancreatitis: imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
CT / MRCP; EUS when malignancy must be excluded.
Recall
Pancreatic-head procedures for chronic pancreatitis: structures at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Portal / SMV confluence or intrapancreatic CBD.
Pancreatic fistula, usually POD 3–7.
Board trap · Automatic WhippleDo not choose Whipple automatically for every chronic pancreatitis patient — the procedure follows duct / head anatomy (duct drainage, Frey or Beger may fit better).

Pancreatic-protocol multidetector CT; 90–95% accuracy for predicting unresectable disease.

🛡️Splenectomy & Splenic Trauma10 items▾

Recall
Kehr sign?
tap to flip
Answer
Left shoulder pain from diaphragmatic irritation; low sensitivity.
Recall
AAST splenic injury grading: range and which grades indicate splenectomy?
tap to flip
Answer
Grade I minor injury → Grade V shattered / devascularized spleen.
Grade IV/V or failed conservative treatment are among the indications for splenectomy.
Recall
Splenic trauma: imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
Hemodynamically stable → contrast CT.
Unstable + positive FAST → do not delay for CT.
Recall
Splenic trauma: OPERATE NOW when?
tap to flip
Answer
Hemodynamic instability from splenic hemorrhage, shattered / devascularized spleen, uncontrolled bleeding, failed NOM / embolization → splenectomy / salvage.
Recall
Stable blunt splenic injury → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Monitored nonoperative management ± splenic arterial embolization — preserve the spleen whenever safely possible.
🩺 Think it through
Blunt trauma patient, hypotensive and exsanguinating, FAST positive, splenic bleeding suspected. CT or operating room?
OR now — no CT. Damage control = rapid splenic hemorrhage control, often splenectomy; definitive care afterwards = vaccination + long-term OPSI prevention.
Board trap · Automatic splenectomy in a stable patientA CT-defined injury — even a high-grade lesion — does not mandate splenectomy when the patient is hemodynamically stable.
Recall
Elective indications for splenectomy?
tap to flip
Answer
Failed medical therapy for ITP, symptomatic hereditary spherocytosis, selected AIHA / hypersplenism, splenic tumor / abscess, symptomatic splenomegaly.
Recall
Splenectomy: laparoscopic or open?
tap to flip
Answer
Laparoscopic when elective and anatomy permits; open for unstable trauma / large hostile spleen as appropriate.
Recall
Splenectomy: classic structure at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Pancreatic tail → pancreatic fistula / subphrenic collection, generally POD 3–7.

  • ✎OPSI risk is lifelong, greatest during the first years after splenectomy.

How does OPSI present?
tap to flip

Fever / viral-like illness → rapidly progressive sepsis, shock, DIC.
Recall
OPSI prevention: which vaccines?
tap to flip

Pneumococcus, meningococcus, Hib; annual influenza vaccination.

tap to flip

Treat as possible OPSI immediately: sepsis treatment + broad-spectrum antimicrobials. Do not wait for culture confirmation.

🧭Decision Frame for the Hepatobiliary–Pancreatic–Splenic Patient4 items▾

  • ★Frame: identify the physiologic emergency first, then decide whether the patient needs urgent decompression / source control, definitive operation, or observation / nonoperative management.
Decision vocabulary
TermMeaningAnswer
Operate / intervene nowAdditional nonessential testing should not delay source control
Damage controlShortest lifesaving intervention for shock, sepsis, hemorrhage, or hostile operative anatomy
Definitive repairCurative or durable operation once physiology and anatomy permit
  • ★POD timings quoted for complications are typical timings, not fixed days.
Recall
Massive liver trauma: damage control vs definitive treatment?
tap to flip
Answer
Damage control: packing ± inflow control.
Definitive: planned re-exploration / definitive vascular / biliary repair.

🌀Colonic Obstruction — Volvulus & Ogilvie Syndrome8 items▾

Volvulus and pseudo-obstruction: decompress, operate, or treat medically
EntityObserve / nonoperativeOPERATE NOWDefinitive procedureDo NOT doAnswer
Sigmoid volvulusViable bowel (coffee-bean, no peritonitis) → DECOMPRESS FIRST: endoscopic detorsion + rectal tubeGangrene / perforation → sigmoid colectomy + end colostomy (Hartmann procedure)Elective sigmoid colectomy after successful detorsionPersist with endoscopy if the bowel is ischemic
Cecal volvulusGenerally none — endoscopic detorsion is generally ineffectiveOnce diagnosed in an operative candidateRight hemicolectomy + ileocolic anastomosisRoutine endoscopic (colonoscopic) detorsion — contraindicated / wrong move
Ogilvie syndromeMedical management when there is no ischemia / perforation: bowel rest → neostigmine / decompressionIschemia / perforationResection if complicatedOperate before excluding mechanical obstruction
🧠 Memory toolSigmoid vs cecal volvulus — first move
SSigmoid = Scope first: detorse the viable sigmoid, then elective sigmoid colectomy
CCecal = Cut: right hemicolectomy; routine endoscopic detorsion is the wrong move
Contrast pair: the same word (volvulus) gets opposite first steps depending on the segment.
Recall
Sigmoid volvulus — named radiologic signs?
tap to flip
Answer
Coffee-bean / bent inner tube on abdominal radiograph; bird-beak sign on contrast enema.
  • ✎After endoscopic detorsion + rectal tube for viable sigmoid volvulus, elective sigmoid colectomy follows because recurrence may reach about %.
  • ★Ogilvie syndrome sequence: exclude mechanical obstruction → stop precipitating drugs, bowel rest, IV hydration → neostigmine 2 mg IV or colonoscopic decompression if persistent.
Recall
Colonic obstruction — imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
CT for most mechanical obstruction; water-soluble contrast may define volvulus / pseudo-obstruction.
Recall
Colonic obstruction → OPERATE NOW when?
tap to flip
Answer
Generalized peritonitis, free perforation, gangrene / ischemic or necrotic bowel, failed decompression, septic deterioration.
No formal operative score: the decision rests on viability, perforation, peritonitis and cause.
Board trap · Colonoscopy in the wrong patientColonoscopy is contraindicated in suspected perforation or near-complete obstruction — tempting as a decompressing or diagnostic step, but the wrong move.

Resuscitation first; localization second.

Painless hematochezia → diverticular / internal hemorrhoidal bleeding.

Brisk active bleeding, not controlled / localized endoscopicallyAngiography → angioembolizeNeeds a minimum bleeding rate; can embolize or infuse vasopressin
  • ✎Angiography localizes a lower GI bleed only when bleeding is approximately mL/min; colonoscopy in the stable patient follows a rapid bowel prep over h.
Recall
Lower GI bleeding → absolute indication to operate?
tap to flip
Answer
Persistent life-threatening hemorrhage despite endoscopic / angiographic control; unstable ongoing colonic bleeding; persistent shock / transfusion dependence despite less invasive therapy.
Recall
Persistent lower GI bleed with a localized site → operation?
tap to flip
Answer
Segmental colectomy — definitive, and only when the bleeding site is localized.
🩺 Think it through
A patient with ongoing colonic hemorrhage remains unstable despite endoscopic and angiographic attempts, and the bleeding site is still unlocalized. Which operation?
Rare subtotal colectomy, after excluding a distal anorectal bleeding site. A segmental resection is reserved for a localized bleed.
Board trap · Blind segmental colectomyRemoving a colonic segment for an unlocalized bleed is contraindicated — never do a blind segmental resection.
  • ✎Top complication after endoscopic control of a lower GI bleed: early rebleeding at .

PresentationManagementAnswer

tap to flip

Supratentorial → seizure / focal deficit.
Infratentorial → hydrocephalus, ataxia, cranial-nerve deficits.

tap to flip

MRI brain with and without gadolinium.

tap to flip

Symptomatic edema → dexamethasone.
Antiseizure treatment if a seizure has occurred.

Schwannoma: point tenderness + shooting pain on palpation.
Malignancy: constant spontaneous pain + motor/sensory deficit.

tap to flip
Answer
MRI with contrast.

TumorAnatomy / clueManagementAnswer

Schwannoma: when is observation acceptable?
tap to flip
Answer
Asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic (small) schwannoma tightly involving a critical nerve — may be followed or subtotally treated. Need to operate NOW is rare.
Board trap · Benign schwannoma on a critical nerveTempting: complete excision at any price. Contraindicated: sacrificing a critical functional nerve merely to achieve complete excision of a benign schwannoma when safe subtotal treatment is reasonable.

tap to flip

Parent nerve/root or spinal cord.
  • ✎After spinal tumor surgery: spinal epidural hematoma is the top early complication, POD ; CSF leak occurs in the .

Obstructive hydrocephalus is seen on CT and the patient's consciousness is now declining with signs of herniation. What must be done?
Operate / drain NOW — external ventricular drain (ventriculostomy), the procedure of choice for acute CSF decompression, or decompression of the lesion.

tap to flip

🩺 Think it through
Head-injured patient with an EDH is actively herniating; formal neurosurgery is unavailable. What can be done now, and what is definitive?
Emergency burr-hole decompression may bridge the life-threatening EDH → formal craniotomy and hemostasis as definitive treatment.
Board trap · Repeat CT in a herniating patientTempting: serial/repeat imaging first. Contraindicated: delaying evacuation for repeat imaging in a clinically herniating patient.
Board trap · Awake patient, thick SDHTempting: observe because GCS is high. Contraindicated: assuming an awake patient with a >1-cm SDH can be observed solely because the GCS is high.
Recall
Chronic SDH → when to drain, and how?
tap to flip
Answer
>1 cm OR symptomatic (significant decline) → burr-hole drainage. Small asymptomatic selected lesions may be observed.
Recall
Chronic SDH: when is open craniotomy needed?
tap to flip
Answer
If too organized, membranes prevent drainage, or bleeding cannot be controlled. Do NOT do craniotomy first in every case.
  • ✎After burr-hole drainage of a chronic SDH, the drain is commonly left for days.
  • ✎Recurrent postoperative hematoma: POD . Delayed traumatic intraparenchymal hemorrhage: highest concern in the first h.

CNS infections: when to operate
ConditionImaging / clueAbsolute operative indicationProcedureAnswer

Subdural empyemaFever + headache + seizure/focal deficit; contrast CT/MRIThe diagnosis itself generally demands urgent drainageWide craniotomy/hemicraniectomy + lavage (wide drainage)

  • ✎Brain abscess that fails to shrink after about of antibiotics → .
Recall
Brain abscess: which may be treated with antibiotics alone?
tap to flip
Answer
Selected small, multiple, or critically located abscesses — culture/biopsy still desirable.
Recall
Spinal epidural abscess: nonoperative management only if…?
tap to flip
Answer
No neurologic deficit + organism known + extremely close monitoring.
Recall
Signs that nonoperative management of a CNS infection has failed?
tap to flip
Answer
New weakness, enlargement, worsening sepsis or mental status.
🩺 Think it through
Back pain + fever + progressive weakness; MRI shows a spinal epidural abscess. What is the decision?
A neurologic emergency — decompress NOW (laminectomy/decompression + culture). Antibiotics alone for a neurologically deteriorating spinal epidural abscess, or delay with progressive weakness, is contraindicated.
Board trap · Subdural empyemaTempting: antibiotics alone. Right: operate NOW — urgent surgical drainage; there is no routine nonoperative management.
Board trap · Lumbar puncture with mass effectContraindicated: LP when intracranial mass effect is suspected — no LP before imaging in a focal intracranial mass syndrome (including brain abscess with mass effect).
  • ★CNS infection + mass effect: antibiotics + urgent decompression (bridge) → complete source control + prolonged antibiotics (definitive).
Recall
Subdural empyema with contralateral hemiparesis — mechanism?
tap to flip
Answer
Cortical vascular thrombosis.
  • ✎Subdural empyema: complications are seizures/hemiparesis; mortality %.
Recall
After drainage of a CNS infection: when does reaccumulation/infection appear?
tap to flip
Answer
From the first several days to weeks.

tap to flip

DecisionWhenAnswer
ObserveMild cataract without meaningful functional impairment

Board trap · Snellen cut-off for cataract surgeryTempting: operate at a fixed visual-acuity number. Right: the operative threshold is functional visual disability; surgery based solely on a predetermined Snellen cut-off without considering function is contraindicated.

  • ★No specific named sign determines operability in lung cancer; presentation may include cough, hemoptysis, weight loss and postobstructive symptoms.

T1≤3 cm
T2>3–5 cm
T3>5–7 cm

Each step up adds 2 cm: 3 → 5 → 7. T size cut-offs are unchanged in the 9th edition; what changed is N2 (split into N2a / N2b) and M1c (split into M1c1 / M1c2).

Board trap · FIGO 2009 vs FIGO 2023Classic textbook (FIGO 2009) staged by anatomy alone: IA <½ myometrial invasion, IB ≥½, II cervix, III serosa / adnexa / vagina / nodes, IVA bladder / bowel mucosa, IVB distant. FIGO 2023 adds histology and LVSI: aggressive histology (high-grade endometrioid, serous, clear cell, carcinosarcoma) with any myometrial invasion = IIC; substantial LVSI = IIB; ovarian / tubal spread is IIIA1, serosa IIIA2.

After a fracture, a patient has pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch of the limb. What is the diagnosis and what must be done?
Compartment syndrome → emergency fasciotomy of all involved compartments, now. The indication is clinical compartment syndrome or the diagnostic ΔP threshold; no imaging is required when the diagnosis is clinically evident.
Compartment perfusion pressure (ΔP)
ΔP = diastolic BP − compartment pressure
ΔP ≤30 mmHg → fasciotomy.

PPulselessness — late

Nongonococcal septic arthritis requiring source control = absolute operative indication → arthrotomy + irrigation/debridement ± drain.
Recall
Which septic arthritis is usually NOT operated?
tap to flip
Answer
Gonococcal arthritis — often treated medically with ceftriaxone ± aspiration; acceptable when it responds.
Board trap · Antibiotics alone for a septic jointWrong move: prolonged antibiotic-only treatment of destructive nongonococcal septic arthritis without drainage. Top complication: rapid cartilage destruction / secondary degenerative joint disease.
Recall
Necrotizing orthopedic infection → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Radical debridement now — imaging must not delay surgery.

👶Pediatric Inguinal Hernia & Hydrocele6 items▾

Pediatric inguinal hernia — presentation → decision
PresentationFindingDecisionAnswer
Reducible (pediatric indirect hernia)Intermittent groin bulgeElective high ligation
IncarceratedFirm nonreducing massSuccessful reduction → repair within roughly 24 h / next available operative slot; failed reduction = emergency
StrangulatedAdds tenderness / skin changes / toxicityOperate now — emergency hernia exploration
Irreducible ovary—Operate now
Recall
Pediatric inguinal hernia — imaging and scoring?
tap to flip
Answer
Clinical diagnosis; imaging usually unnecessary. No scoring system.
Recall
Pediatric inguinal hernia — procedure of choice and structures at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
High ligation of the patent processus vaginalis.
At risk: vas deferens and testicular vessels.
  • ✎After pediatric hernia repair: scrotal edema/hematoma POD ; recurrence .
  • ✎Isolated hydrocele in an infant without hernia: observe for at least the first months (EAU/ESPU) — most resolve spontaneously; many surgeons wait until 12–24 months before repair.
Board trap · Watchful waiting for a child's herniaWrong move: long-term watchful waiting for a true pediatric inguinal hernia — every confirmed pediatric inguinal hernia ultimately requires repair.

🫁Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia8 items▾

Recall
CDH “honeymoon period”?
tap to flip
Answer
Transient early stability before cardiopulmonary deterioration.
🩺 Think it through
A neonate in respiratory distress has bowel in the chest. Operate now?
CDH — No (unless another surgical catastrophe exists). Stabilize first, repair later: all repairable CDH eventually requires repair, but only after physiologic stabilization. This is not observation of the lesion — it is physiologic stabilization before repair.
  • ★CDH management ladder: stabilize first — gentle ventilation, OG/NG decompression, treat pulmonary hypertension → HFOV ± nitric oxide/inotropes → ECMO for refractory hypoxemia in suitable patients → diaphragm repair once hemodynamics/pulmonary pressures are optimized.
  • ✎CDH permissive hypercapnia: PaCO₂ ~ mmHg, or higher if pH ≥.
Recall
CDH — imaging?
tap to flip
Answer
Chest X-ray; echocardiography for pulmonary hypertension/cardiac defects.
Recall
CDH repair — procedure and structures at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
Primary diaphragmatic closure; prosthetic patch for a large defect.
At risk during reduction: spleen and liver.
Recall
CDH — top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Hemothorax/bleeding on ECMO; recurrence is a later concern.
Board trap · Rushing CDH to the ORContraindicated: immediate repair of an unstable CDH before cardiopulmonary stabilization.

🍼Esophageal Atresia / Tracheoesophageal Fistula8 items▾

🧠 Memory toolVACTERL association (with EA/TEF)
VVertebral
AAnorectal
CCardiac
TETracheo-Esophageal
RRenal
LLimb
Also written VACTERRL — the extra R splits Renal and Radial (limb).
Recall
Classic sign and imaging of EA/TEF?
tap to flip
Answer
OG tube cannot pass and coils in the proximal pouch; distal bowel gas suggests a distal TEF.
Imaging: plain chest/abdominal radiograph with the tube in place.
🩺 Think it through
A drooling newborn has a tube coiled in the upper pouch. What is done first, and when is the repair?
EA/TEF. Initial management: head elevated ≥30° + continuous pouch suction + NPO + IV fluids/antibiotics. Stabilize → repair; a stable infant usually undergoes repair within 1–2 days, not instant delivery-room surgery.
Recall
EA/TEF — procedure of choice and structures at risk?
tap to flip
Answer
TEF ligation/division + primary esophagoesophageal anastomosis.
At risk: trachea, esophageal blood supply, azygos/RLN.
Recall
EA/TEF — operative indication, and what if the infant is an unstable premature with severe distention?
tap to flip
Answer
Definitive repair in a suitable infant; severe gastric distention/ventilatory compromise may require urgent decompression.
Unstable premature infant with severe distention → damage control: pouch suction ± temporary gastrostomy; definitive = fistula ligation + esophageal anastomosis.
  • ✎EA/TEF repair: anastomotic leak ; major (catastrophic) early leak POD → .
  • ✎Late complication of EA/TEF repair: anastomotic stricture — the most common; classic textbook , contemporary series report more (about 40–60% need dilation), often weeks–months, treated with .
Board trap · Bagging a TEF babyContraindicated: aggressive positive-pressure bag-mask ventilation — it forces air through the distal fistula into the stomach.

🎗️Pediatric Tumors — Wilms Tumor & Neuroblastoma11 items▾

Wilms tumor staging
StageExtentBoard decisionAnswer
IKidney only, completely excisedNephroureterectomy + nodes + adjuvant chemotherapy (vincristine + dactinomycin); very low risk (age <2 years, tumor <550 g, nodes negative) → nephrectomy alone (COG)
IIBeyond kidney, completely excisedSame operative principle + stage-directed therapy
IIIResidual abdominal disease, nodes, spillage/biopsy, positive marginIntensified chemo ± radiation
IVHematogenous / distant nodesSystemic multimodality therapy
VBilateral kidneysBiopsy + preop chemotherapy → nephron-sparing surgery
Board trap · Spilling a Wilms tumorTumor rupture/spillage → at least Stage III. Wrong move: careless biopsy/rupture of an otherwise resectable unilateral Wilms tumor.
Recall
Wilms tumor — imaging of choice?
tap to flip
Answer
CT abdomen + chest; ultrasound for renal-vein/IVC extension.
Recall
Resectable unilateral Wilms tumor → operation?
tap to flip
Answer
Absolute operative indication → radical nephroureterectomy + regional lymph-node sampling.
Recall
Wilms tumor — indications for preoperative chemotherapy?
tap to flip
Answer
Bilateral disease, solitary kidney, IVC extension above the hepatic veins.
Recall
Wilms nephrectomy — structure at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Renal pedicle / IVC.
Hemorrhage, POD 0–2.
Recall
Neuroblastoma — markers and the poor-prognosis marker?
tap to flip
Answer
Urine/serum VMA/HVA.
N-MYC amplification = poor prognosis.
🧠 Memory toolINRG staging of neuroblastoma
L1Localized, no image-defined risk factor (IDRF)
L2Locoregional + IDRF
MDistant metastatic
MS<18 months, limited to skin / liver / marrow
L = local, M = metastatic, S = special.
Recall
Neuroblastoma — imaging?
tap to flip
Answer
CT/MRI + metastatic staging; marrow/radionuclide studies.
Recall
Neuroblastoma — when to resect, when not?
tap to flip
Answer
Localized resectable disease → complete resection when safe.
Unresectable/high-risk → biopsy + chemotherapy first.
Recall
Neuroblastoma resection — structures at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Major retroperitoneal vessels / renal pedicles / neural foramina.
Vascular/organ injury; recurrence.

🌀Pediatric Intestinal Obstruction — Volvulus, Atresia, Intussusception, Meconium Ileus14 items▾

Neonatal/infant obstruction — side by side
ConditionNamed signImagingProcedureStructure at riskTop complicationAnswer
Midgut volvulusCorkscrew duodenum on upper-GI study; bilious vomiting = key clinical warningStable child → upper-GI seriesCounterclockwise detorsion + Ladd procedureSMA mesenteric rootBowel necrosis / short-gut syndrome
Duodenal / jejunoileal atresiaDouble bubble = duodenal obstructionPlain abdominal X-ray; contrast only if uncertaintyDuodenoduodenostomy or resection/anastomosis according to levelMesenteric blood supplyAnastomotic leak POD 3–7
IntussusceptionCurrant-jelly stool, Dance signAir enema (imaging and treatment of choice) in stable child without peritonitisSurgical reduction ± resectionBowel wall / mesenteric perfusionRecurrence 5–10%, often early
Meconium ileus“Ground-glass” abdominal filmContrast enema → microcolonIrrigation ± limited ileal resection/stoma/anastomosis——
🩺 Think it through
A neonate with bilious vomiting is deteriorating. What is the diagnosis and the next step?
Midgut volvulus → OR now: immediate laparotomy/laparoscopy + counterclockwise detorsion + Ladd. Suspected/confirmed volvulus is an absolute operative indication, especially in the toxic/tender/unstable child.
Board trap · Imaging the unstable volvulusWrong move: a contrast study that delays operation in unstable suspected volvulus. Critically ill child with bilious emesis and suspected volvulus → operate now; do not delay for further imaging.
Board trap · Wrong way roundContraindicated: clockwise detorsion. The correct direction is counterclockwise — “turn back the hands of time”.
  • ✎Midgut volvulus with extensive questionable ischemia (damage control): detorse, resect only clearly necrotic bowel, second look at ; definitive = Ladd + final bowel resection/reconstruction.
Recall
Duodenal/jejunoileal atresia — when to operate?
tap to flip
Answer
Complete congenital mechanical obstruction → operate after stabilization.
Recall
Colicky infant + currant-jelly stool, stable, no peritonitis → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Intussusception → air enema.
Successful reduction → short observation, then feeds.
  • ✎Air-enema reduction of intussusception: pressure generally ≤ mmHg.
Recall
Intussusception — absolute operative indications?
tap to flip
Answer
Peritonitis, systemic toxicity, perforation/gangrene, failed radiographic reduction → operative reduction ± resection.
Board trap · Air enema with peritonitisContraindicated: air-enema reduction in intussusception with established peritonitis.
Board trap · Pulling the intussusceptumDuring surgical (manual) reduction, push / gently milk the intussusceptum out — do not forcefully pull the bowel.
Recall
Uncomplicated meconium ileus → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Nonoperative: water-soluble contrast / N-acetylcysteine enema.
Recall
Meconium ileus — when to operate?
tap to flip
Answer
Complicated disease, associated atresia, failure of contrast to reflux into the dilated ileum, or failed enema.
Board trap · Hyperosmolar enemasContraindicated: repeated hyperosmolar enemas without aggressive fluid/electrolyte monitoring.

🟡Biliary Atresia7 items▾

Recall
Acholic/pale stool + persistent conjugated jaundice in an infant → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Biliary atresia → expedite cholangiography / Kasai.
  • ✎Kasai before days of age → higher chance of durable bile drainage.
  • ★Biliary atresia work-up: ultrasound (imaging of choice); DISIDA/HIDA as supportive study → operative cholangiography = definitive diagnostic step when the diagnosis remains likely/uncertain → confirmed atresia (absolute operative indication) → Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy, ideally early.
Recall
Can proven biliary atresia be observed? What if Kasai fails?
tap to flip
Answer
No curative observation strategy exists.
Failed bile drainage / progressive cirrhosis / portal hypertension → liver transplantation.
Recall
Kasai — structure at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Portal vein / hepatic artery at the porta hepatis.
Cholangitis, typically weeks–months rather than a fixed POD.
Board trap · Visible gallbladderWrong move: dismissing biliary atresia because the gallbladder is visible on ultrasound — about 10% may still have a visible distal gallbladder.
Board trap · Expecting dilated ductsClassic trap: intrahepatic ducts are not dilated in biliary atresia.

🚼Hirschsprung Disease10 items▾

  • ✎Failure to pass meconium > → investigate for .
Recall
No meconium >48 h + transition zone → diagnosis and plan?
tap to flip
Answer
Hirschsprung → rectal biopsy → pull-through with ganglionated bowel. All confirmed disease ultimately requires surgery.
🧠 Memory toolRectal suction biopsy in Hirschsprung (definitive diagnosis)
1Absent ganglion cells
2Hypertrophied nerves
3↑ AChE
None – big – up.
Board trap · Transition zone ≠ diagnosisContrast enema is the imaging of choice (identifies the transition zone), but treating the transition zone as the definitive diagnosis without biopsy is wrong.
🧠 Memory toolPull-through procedures for Hirschsprung
SSwenson
DDuhamel
SSoave
All use ganglionated bowel.
Board trap · Transition-zone pull-throughWrong: pull-through using transition-zone or aganglionic bowel. Anastomose at least ~5 cm proximal to the first demonstrated ganglion cells.
Recall
Sign of Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis on examination?
tap to flip
Answer
Explosive expulsion of foul liquid stool after rectal examination.
  • ★Stable colon: rectal irrigations to decompress → definitive pull-through once adequately decompressed without uncontrolled enterocolitis; a primary pull-through is acceptable even in neonates when adequately decompressed.
Recall
Hirschsprung enterocolitis or obstruction failing fluids + antibiotics + NG + rectal irrigations → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Diversion now: leveling stoma in ganglionated bowel (damage control: rectal irrigation/antibiotics ± stoma).
Definitive later: pull-through.
Recall
Pull-through — structure at risk and top complication?
tap to flip
Answer
Pelvic parasympathetic/autonomic nerves.
Hirschsprung-associated enterocolitis — may occur early or late.
